messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 25
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 44

When he is seven, the first door slams. It is not an ordinary sound. It is the hinge of a room where the air turns cold. His stepfather, who shares the house with his mother, mistakes a spilled glass for defiance. The first strike does not break skin; it breaks his sense of safety. He learns quickly that silence is armor. He counts ceiling cracks until the shouting stops. He memorizes the rhythm of heavy footsteps, the shift in breathing that always precedes violence. By twelve, his shoulders stay permanently hunched, his eyes dart toward exits before others have noticed a room at all. He carries a quiet terror that has nothing to do with the dark and everything to do with proximity. At seventeen, he packs a duffel bag and takes a bus south. He works odd jobs, then settles into housekeeping. The work makes sense. Dust does not shout. Sheets do not lie. He learns the chemistry of bleach and the geometry of a perfectly made bed. Clients leave him tips in ceramic mugs; he stacks them on a high shelf without using a single one. He tells his coworkers he likes quiet. It is true, but what he means is that quiet does not change its mind mid-sentence. He has learned to read the weight of a space, to know when to step back and when to lean in. At twenty-five, his apartment is sparse. Every object has a designated place. He remains single, not from lack of interest, but from a simple calculus: intimacy requires unpredictability, and he has spent two decades avoiding the unknown. When he works night shifts cleaning hotel corridors, he moves with practiced invisibility. Yet his body keeps the ledger. A dropped tray sends him flat against a wall, heart hammering against his ribs like a trapped bird. He does not tell his supervisor. He checks the exit sign three times, traces the fire escape in his head, and waits for the adrenaline to bleed out of his hands. Sleep is a negotiation. He wakes at three a.m. every night, not from a dream, but from the sudden absence of breath in his own chest. He lies still until the ceiling fan’s rhythm matches his own. He cancels plans when voices rise in nearby apartments. He watches documentaries and feels nothing but a familiar tightness behind his sternum. At work, he notices the small fractures in client homes first—the warped floorboard, the hairline crack in a window pane. He fixes them with careful hands, as if mending them might quiet the older, deeper breaks. Friends say he is distant. He does not argue. Distance is predictable. Distance does not pick locks or lie about why it will be the last time. He washes his hands until the skin maps itself in fine white lines. He counts the suds to ten, then rinses. The water runs clear. Outside, a car backfires. He does not look up. He just sets the towel down, smooths the crease with his thumb, and waits for the next room to clean.
